analysis.one_liner: Repeals all corporate, estate, and gift taxes and replaces the individual income tax with a 10 percent tax on wages only.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: one senator introduced it with no cosponsors, and the Senate Finance Committee let it expire when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the corporate income tax, the estate tax, the gift tax, and taxes on insurers, mutual funds, and real estate trusts. In their place, it would tax only money people earn from working — wages and self-employment income — at a flat 10 percent above a $10,000 exemption. Money from wealth would go untaxed: no tax on capital gains, interest, rent, dividends (except a narrow case), or inheritances. It also repeals virtually every deduction and credit individuals use today.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations would stop paying federal income tax entirely. Families inheriting large estates would pay nothing to transfer wealth. Wealthy households living on investments — dividends, interest, rents, capital gains — would pay no income tax at all, since the bill taxes only wages and self-employment earnings. Insurers, mutual funds, and real estate trusts would be freed from the taxes they currently pay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations, wealthy investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the corporate income tax and related corporate taxes, including taxes on foreign corporations earning U.S. income, accumulated earnings, personal holding companies, and insurers, mutual funds, and real estate trusts.
Replaces the individual income tax with a 10 percent tax on earned income above a $10,000 exemption, indexed to inflation.
Taxes only wages and self-employment earnings; pensions, annuities, and most tips are excluded, and investment income is not taxed.
Repeals the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax entirely.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the entire income tax burden would fall on people who work for wages or run small businesses, while income from wealth and corporate profits would go untaxed. Federal revenue would drop sharply, forcing either large cuts to public programs, deficits, or some other tax to fill the gap.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals all specific individual tax exclusions, deductions, and credits, ending benefits like the earned income credit and deductions for home mortgage interest, state and local taxes, and charitable giving.

Because it taxes only earned income, a household living off investments or inheritance would pay nothing, while a working family above the exemption would pay on every wage dollar — a shift of the tax burden onto labor and away from wealth.

Eliminating corporate, estate, gift, and insurer/fund taxes would cut federal revenue drastically; the bill specifies no replacement revenue and only directs Treasury to draft technical changes, implying major deficits or program cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's simplicity — one low rate on wages — would benefit some working people with high wages and no itemized deductions. But its design gives away the entire corporate and estate tax base and leaves investment income untouched, so the cost of funding the government would shift onto workers alone. The larger your income from wealth rather than work, the more you gain; the more you depend on a paycheck, the more you bear. Any serious tax reform that eliminated corporate and estate taxes would need to say where the money comes from; this bill does not.

outcome.mechanism: One senator introduced it, no one joined him, the Finance Committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Helms introduced the bill in the Senate on October 31, 1991.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which held no further proceedings on it.
The bill received no vote in either chamber and expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary wage earners kept the existing tax structure — corporations still pay income tax, large estates still face the estate tax, and investment income is still taxed. The companies and wealthy families who would have gained from the bill got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wage earners; the tax code stayed unchanged

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by Sen. Lloyd Bentsen (D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never held hearings, marked it up, or reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: All 100 senators
against.what_they_did: No senator cosponsored the bill during its two-plus years pending.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a solo Republican proposal with no cosponsors from either party and died in committee without a vote, so the record shows no organized support or opposition beyond the sponsor.

industries.industry: Corporations, including foreign corporations with U.S. income
industries.note: The bill repeals the corporate income tax and related corporate taxes entirely, shifting the revenue burden onto wages. Ordinary workers would bear the cost of replacing that revenue.

industries.industry: Life insurers, other insurers, mutual funds, and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill repeals the specific tax regimes covering these industries, freeing them from federal income tax on their earnings.

industries.industry: Wealthy estates, inheritors, and high-income investment households
industries.note: Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes, combined with taxing only earned income, means large fortunes and investment income would pass and grow untaxed, while workers pay 10 percent on wages.
